items.stem: By late 2021, roughly what share of people in low-income countries had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, compared with over 60 per cent in high-income countries?
items.answer: Under 10 per cent
items.markingKey: D. The gap was described by the WHO Director-General as “vaccine apartheid”.

items.stem: Distinguish between health as a human right and health security.
items.answer: Health security focuses on protecting populations, often in rich states, from cross-border outbreaks; health as a right focuses on every individual’s entitlement to the highest attainable standard of health, including care for non-communicable disease.
items.markingKey: Health security focuses on protecting populations, often in rich states, from cross-border outbreaks; health as a right focuses on every individual’s entitlement to the highest attainable standard of health, including care for non-communicable disease. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Freya writes: "Global health is only about infectious disease." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Non-communicable diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes cause around 74 per cent of deaths worldwide and are increasingly political issues (tobacco and sugar regulation).
items.markingKey: Non-communicable diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes cause around 74 per cent of deaths worldwide and are increasingly political issues (tobacco and sugar regulation). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the West African Ebola outbreak (2014–16) as an example, explain health security and state capacity.
items.answer: Weak health systems in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were overwhelmed; the WHO was criticised for declaring a PHEIC only in August 2014, and the UN created its first emergency health mission (UNMEER). The outbreak showed that weak health systems threaten regional and global security, and that global institutions depended on state cooperation and funding.
items.markingKey: Context (Weak health systems in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were overwhelmed; the WHO was criticised for declaring a PHEIC only in August 2014, and the UN created its first emergency health mission (UNMEER).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The outbreak showed that weak health systems threaten regional and global security, and that global institutions depended on state cooperation and funding. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to health security and state capacity.

items.stem:
Source C
The world has failed to share vaccines fairly. Rich countries have bought up most of the supply while health workers and vulnerable people in poorer countries remain unprotected. This is not only a moral failure; it prolongs the pandemic for everyone.
— Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, speech (2021) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source C about health as a global political issue. [3]
items.answer: vaccines have not been shared fairly; rich countries bought most of the supply; unequal access prolongs the pandemic for everyone
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: vaccines have not been shared fairly; rich countries bought most of the supply; unequal access prolongs the pandemic for everyone. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Treating health as a security issue has improved global responses to disease."
items.answer: Securitisation has mobilised resources for outbreaks, but at the cost of a narrow, state-centred view of health.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Resolution 1308 increased funding for HIV/AIDS; Ebola Resolution 2177 mobilised UNMEER; pandemic preparedness funding after COVID-19. Arguments against: focus on rich states’ fears; border closures and rights restrictions; neglects non-communicable disease and primary care. Supported judgement: Securitisation has mobilised resources for outbreaks, but at the cost of a narrow, state-centred view of health.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "access to medicines"?
options: The WTO Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (1994), which requires members to grant patents, including on medicines, for at least 20 years
A government authorising the production of a patented product, such as a medicine, without the patent holder’s consent, in return for compensation, permitted under TRIPS
The ability of people to obtain affordable, safe and effective medicines, shaped by prices, patents, health systems and trade rules
A group of infectious diseases, such as schistosomiasis and dengue, that mainly affect the poorest populations and receive little research funding
items.answer: The ability of people to obtain affordable, safe and effective medicines, shaped by prices, patents, health systems and trade rules
items.markingKey: C. "access to medicines" is the ability of people to obtain affordable, safe and effective medicines, shaped by prices, patents, health systems and trade rules.

items.stem: Explain why states may delay reporting disease outbreaks.
items.answer: Reporting can bring travel and trade restrictions, economic losses and reputational damage, so governments may hide or downplay outbreaks, as China did with SARS in 2002–03.

items.answer: COVID-19 death rates and economic harm fell more heavily on poorer, minority and informal-sector workers, and poorer states had slower access to vaccines.

items.stem: Distinguish between assessed contributions to the WHO and voluntary contributions.

items.stem: With reference to COVID-19 vaccine distribution (2021), explain how it illustrates vaccine nationalism and global inequality.
items.answer: High-income states secured most early vaccine supplies through advance purchase deals while COVAX struggled to deliver doses to low-income countries. States prioritised national interest, illustrating realist behaviour and unequal power in access to medicines.
items.markingKey: Context (High-income states secured most early vaccine supplies through advance purchase deals while COVAX struggled to deliver doses to low-income countries.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: States prioritised national interest, illustrating realist behaviour and unequal power in access to medicines. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to vaccine nationalism and global inequality.

items.stem:
Source D
We agree that the TRIPS Agreement does not and should not prevent members from taking measures to protect public health. The Agreement can and should be interpreted in a manner supportive of members’ right to protect public health and, in particular, to promote access to medicines for all.
— WTO Doha Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and Public Health (2001), paragraph 4 (extract)

Identify three commitments made in Source D. [3]
items.answer: TRIPS should not prevent measures to protect public health; TRIPS should be interpreted to support the right to protect public health; access to medicines should be promoted for all
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: TRIPS should not prevent measures to protect public health; TRIPS should be interpreted to support the right to protect public health; access to medicines should be promoted for all. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem:
Source A
Gavi has helped to immunise more than one billion children and to prevent millions of future deaths. By pooling demand and providing predictable funding, it has created healthy markets for vaccines and reduced prices for the poorest countries.
— Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, Annual Progress Report (2023) (adapted)

With reference to Source A, explain why the source might be seen as presenting a partial view. [4]
items.answer: It is the organisation’s own report, so it emphasises successes and may omit criticisms such as donor influence, accountability gaps or vaccine shortfalls during COVID-19.
items.markingKey: It is the organisation’s own report, so it emphasises successes and may omit criticisms such as donor influence, accountability gaps or vaccine shortfalls during COVID-19. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Examine the view that treating health as a security issue has improved global responses to disease. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Securitisation has mobilised resources for outbreaks, but at the cost of a narrow, state-centred view of health.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: Resolution 1308 increased funding for HIV/AIDS; Ebola Resolution 2177 mobilised UNMEER; pandemic preparedness funding after COVID-19. Arguments against: focus on rich states’ fears; border closures and rights restrictions; neglects non-communicable disease and primary care. Possible judgement: Securitisation has mobilised resources for outbreaks, but at the cost of a narrow, state-centred view of health. items.stem: Define the term "International Health Regulations (2005)".
items.answer: The legally binding instrument requiring WHO member states to develop core public health capacities and report events that may constitute a PHEIC
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the legally binding instrument requiring WHO member states to develop core public health capacities and report events that may constitute a PHEIC. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A group of infectious diseases, such as schistosomiasis and dengue, that mainly affect the poorest populations and receive little research funding"?
items.answer: neglected tropical diseases
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of neglected tropical diseases.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "compulsory licensing".
items.answer: A government authorising the production of a patented product, such as a medicine, without the patent holder’s consent, in return for compensation, permitted under TRIPS
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a government authorising the production of a patented product, such as a medicine, without the patent holder’s consent, in return for compensation, permitted under TRIPS. items.stem: Briefly explain why the US relationship with the WHO matters for global health governance.
items.answer: The USA has been the largest state funder; its announced withdrawals in 2020 and 2025 cut resources and influence, showing the dependence of global institutions on powerful states.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The USA has been the largest state funder; its announced withdrawals in 2020 and 2025 cut resources and influence, showing the dependence of global institutions on powerful states. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Maya writes: "Pandemics affect all populations equally." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: COVID-19 death rates and economic harm fell more heavily on poorer, minority and informal-sector workers, and poorer states had slower access to vaccines.
items.markingKey: COVID-19 death rates and economic harm fell more heavily on poorer, minority and informal-sector workers, and poorer states had slower access to vaccines. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the TRIPS waiver of 2022 was seen as disappointing by campaigners.
items.answer: It came late, applied only to vaccines and not treatments or diagnostics, did not cover know-how and technology transfer, and was opposed for months by the EU, UK and Switzerland.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It came late, applied only to vaccines and not treatments or diagnostics, did not cover know-how and technology transfer, and was opposed for months by the EU, UK and Switzerland. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between horizontal health system strengthening and vertical health programmes.
items.answer: Vertical programmes target specific diseases (e.g. polio eradication); horizontal approaches build general health systems, workforces and primary care.
items.markingKey: Vertical programmes target specific diseases (e.g. polio eradication); horizontal approaches build general health systems, workforces and primary care. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the securitisation of health has been criticised.
items.answer: Framing disease as a security threat can prioritise rich states’ protection from outbreaks over the everyday health needs of the poor, and can justify border closures and restrictions on rights.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Framing disease as a security threat can prioritise rich states’ protection from outbreaks over the everyday health needs of the poor, and can justify border closures and restrictions on rights. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The right to health means governments must provide free health care to everyone immediately." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It requires progressive realisation using maximum available resources, with core obligations such as non-discrimination and access to essential medicines.
items.markingKey: It requires progressive realisation using maximum available resources, with core obligations such as non-discrimination and access to essential medicines. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the West African Ebola outbreak (2014–16) and explain what it reveals about health security and state capacity.
items.answer: Weak health systems in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were overwhelmed; the WHO was criticised for declaring a PHEIC only in August 2014, and the UN created its first emergency health mission (UNMEER). The outbreak showed that weak health systems threaten regional and global security, and that global institutions depended on state cooperation and funding.
items.markingKey: Context (Weak health systems in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were overwhelmed; the WHO was criticised for declaring a PHEIC only in August 2014, and the UN created its first emergency health mission (UNMEER).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The outbreak showed that weak health systems threaten regional and global security, and that global institutions depended on state cooperation and funding. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to health security and state capacity.

items.stem: With reference to the South African HIV/AIDS medicines case (1998–2001), explain how it illustrates access to medicines and the power of civil society.
items.answer: Thirty-nine pharmaceutical firms sued South Africa over a law allowing parallel imports of cheaper medicines; under global public pressure from activists, they withdrew the case in 2001. Activists reframed patents as a human-rights issue, forcing companies to retreat and paving the way for the Doha Declaration.
items.markingKey: Context (Thirty-nine pharmaceutical firms sued South Africa over a law allowing parallel imports of cheaper medicines; under global public pressure from activists, they withdrew the case in 2001.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Activists reframed patents as a human-rights issue, forcing companies to retreat and paving the way for the Doha Declaration. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to access to medicines and the power of civil society.

items.stem: With reference to the WHO response to COVID-19, explain how it illustrates the limits of global health institutions.
items.answer: The WHO declared a PHEIC in January 2020 and coordinated scientific guidance, but faced criticism for initial deference to China, and the USA announced withdrawal in 2020 (reversed in 2021) and again in 2025. The WHO’s dependence on state cooperation and funding constrained its independence, illustrating the tension between sovereignty and global governance.
